newsitem.title: USA: Mass suicide prompts jokes, satire.
newsitem.headline: Mass suicide prompts jokes, satire.

text.p: The Heaven's Gate mass suicide prompted shock, horror -- and the inevitable jokes. Lots of jokes.
Despite the tragic nature of the event, comedians found it fair game for a broadside of puns, parody and satire.
" ... It was the biggest suicide in San Diego since the Republicans nominated Bob Dole" to run for president, Jay Leno of NBC television's "Tonight Show" cracked in a recent monologue.
"Let's just hope this isolated incident doesn't give cults a bad name," Leno said.
Last week's discovery of the bodies of 39 men and women in a mansion in Rancho Santa Fe near San Diego and the revelations that followed sparked more jokes, some in bad taste.
A nearly identical copy of the cult's spacey Web site says:
"Once again, some idiots have gotten the idea that putting a bag over your head is the way to God" -- a reference to the plastic bags used in the suicides.

The jokes seemed to be an attempt to cope with horror through laughter, like the quips that followed other tragedies, such as the execution-suicides of 911 followers of the Rev. Jim Jones' cult in Guyana in 1978.
Indeed, one joke repeatedly turning up on the Internet says the Heaven's Gate members killed themselves in order "to keep up with the Joneses."

Details that emerged in the case provided ample fuel for jokes, from the black Nike sneakers on the bodies shown in TV footage (one Web site added the advertising slogan: "Just Do It" to the picture) to the mansion where the cult members lived.
One editorial cartoon showed an affluent Rancho Santa Fe resident reading a newspaper and informing his wife, "They were renters."
"Thank God," she replies.
Some linked Heaven's Gate leader Marshall Applewhite's cult name, Do, to TV cartoon character Homer Simpson's famed utterance: "D'oh!"

Some of the material was inspired by the discovery that some male cultists had been castrated and that all believed the comet Hale-Bopp heralded the arrival of an alien spaceship that would take them to a "level above human."
"You had to castrate yourself to get on the spaceship?" asked Leno. "You thought there was no leg room in coach (class)."

Another inspiration for comics were the news reports that focused on the group's Web site, which laid out their millennial, science fiction-flavored theology, and the work they did to support themselves, which was Web site design.

Anyone with a little technical expertise, the right software and Net access can put up a Web page about anything -- and Heaven's Gate was no exception. Some "Netizens" used the cult's site and the Higher Source site the group used to promote its business as springboards for parody.
Yahoo, a popular catalogue of the Web, had a growing list of Heaven's Gate humour sites that by Thursday had grown to at least 10.

One joke site declared tongue in cheek that the cult members killed themselves because they had viewed a video of the movie "Heaven's Gate" -- a Western that is legendary in Hollywood as a financial disaster -- 300 times.
"I would have done the same thing," the site says.

At a site parodying the real Higher Source site, a bald man clothed in a purple robe -- like the shrouds that draped the cult member's bodies -- beams out from a circular sunbeam logo surrounded by the words "HIGHERSOURCE.ORG ... We kill ourselves working for you." Computer users with the right equipment can hear the song "Suicide is Painless" from the 1970 movie "M*A*S*H" playing in the background.
The Mr. Showbiz celebrity and entertainment site invited users to craft their own Heaven's Gate haiku. By late Thursday morning, there were dozens of entries.
Mr. Showbiz gave some examples to spark creativity, including:
"Why the black Nikes?
If the aliens are mean,
We'll run away quick."

Several Heaven's Gate humour Web sites are listed under Yahoo's broad Society and Culture: Religion category. The list can be found at http://www.yahoo.com/Society_and_Culture/Religion/Humor/Heaven_s_Gate/
Mr. Showbiz's home page, with a link to the Haiku section, can be found at http://www.mrshowbiz.com
The Higher Source parody page is at http://www.highersource.org
The Heaven's Gate cult parody page is at http://www.skylinestudios.com/starbuck/heavensgate.html
